5018.dq: Primary stress is assigned to the penultimate (second last) vowel of a word with secondary stress on every second vowel to the left.
5018.heavy: Not stated as weight by the source; stated as vowel counting: 'Sequences of two identical vowels /ii/, /ee/, /aa/, /oo/ and /uu/ are usually each realized as a single phonetically long vowel.... such reduced double vowels still bear primary stress, as expected for penultimate vowels.' Equivalent heavy syllable = one containing a double (long) vowel or two-vowel sequence (VV); closed CVC syllables are not heavy (fulan [ˈfʊla̟n], tikan [ˈtikæn] keep penult stress).
5018.prule: As stated: primary stress on the penultimate vowel of the word, every vowel counting one, a phonemic double vowel /ii ee aa oo uu/ (realized as one long vowel) counting as two; so a word-final double vowel carries primary stress (kiis-aan [ˌkiːˈsaˑŋ] 'teeth', iluk-aan [ˌʔɪlʊˈkaŋ] 'nose', ikim-aan [ˌʔɪkiˈmaŋ] 'chin', oet-aat [ʔɔɛˈt̪æːt̪] 'vein', hare wee [ˌharˈβ̞ɛː] 'wet rice field') while words with a short final vowel stress the penultimate syllable (fulan [ˈfʊla̟n] 'moon', tikan [ˈtikæn] 'year', lobu [ˈlobʊ] 'mud', isa [ˈʔisa] 'one'). On surface syllables (the catalog's unit): stress the final syllable if it contains a double/long vowel (CVV), otherwise the penult; closed CVC finals are not heavy. Cued by higher pitch and length.
5018.srule: Secondary stress on every second vowel to the left of the primary (binary alternation leftward, counted in vowels; a double vowel counts two): ulit-aat [ˌʔʊlˑˈt̪æt̪] 'skin', iluk-aan [ˌʔɪlʊˈkaŋ] 'nose', usan milis [ˌʔʊsa̟nˈmɪlɪs] 'drizzle'; with the suffix allomorphs -aan/-aat the bare stem's stressed syllable keeps a secondary stress (p. 39).

5019.prule: No fixed syllable. Stress is grammatically conditioned (conservative Romani 'grammatical stress'): inherited inflected words carry the chief stress on the inflectional ending / final syllable (givéskō, guruvá, ṗalá, devél, gonṓ, bakaré, puredér), athematic loans keep a non-final stress (kirčíma, lovína), and words left unaccented in Sampson's transcription are first-stressed by his stated convention. Position shifts with grammatical function: demonstratives are oxytone as pronouns and paroxytone as adjectives (okóva mūrš vs okovā́ sī ō mūrš); imperatives sing. of -d/-t stems in -dē/-tē are stem-stressed (tā́rdē); nouns/adjectives are final-stressed when predicative and initial-stressed elsewhere (Sampson 1926: 23-28 as summarised by Matras 2002: 64; one first-hand instance on p. 17: title Dinilō vs predicative Dinilṓ sas yek ṗal).

5020.prule: No word-stress or accent rule is stated anywhere in the source. Wemɛgbe is described as a two-tone language: underlying /H/ vs /B/ (= L), with surface M, BH (rising) and HB (falling) derived by rule; realisation is conditioned by the voicing of the root-initial consonant (voiceless obstruents insert a consonantal H and block spreading of a floating prefixal B' tone) and, for M, by a following H.
5020.srule: Not mentioned in Gbéto 2004 (SAL 33(1): 65-90, whole article read): the source is a tonology and says nothing about stress of any degree.
5020.quote: In this paper I show that Wemɛgbe, a language spoken in southern Benin, has two underlying tones, H and L, and that the surface tones M, LH and HL are derived by phonological rules. A H tone is inserted after an initial prevocalic voiceless obstruent (occurring in non verbals), creating a HL contour tone, when the vowel of the syllable is L toned. The LH tone is derived through a right-spreading rule from a L' prefix tone, which is postulated for all verbs in their imperative forms and for all nouns. [p. 65] ... On est donc en droit de dire que le wemɛgbe oppose un ton H à un ton non H, symbo…
5020.loc: Abstract, p. 65; §6.1 'Hypothèse de deux tons de base: H et B', pp. 77-78; §7 Conclusion, p. 85

5020.tone: The source is a synchronic tonology and says nothing about stress or accent: a full-text search for accent/stress/intensité/proéminence/emphase/prosod/tonique hits only the diacritic conventions on p. 66 ('le ton B(as) par un accent grave, le ton H(aut) par un accent aigu') and 'niveau prosodique' in fn. 16 p. 85 (tonal correspondences of two numerals). Tone system as stated: two tonemes /H/ and /B/ (§6.1, pp. 77-78; §7, p. 85); M is /B/ before H and occurs only in polysyllabic radicals (fn. 10, p. 77); BH is /H/ after a voiced consonant via spreading of a prefixal B' tone posited for all nouns and imperative verbs; HB (nominals only) is /B/ after a voiceless obstruent via insertion of a consonantal H; the paper argues root-initial consonants are TBUs (abstract, p. 65; p. 86).

[p. 71] … Dans la mesure ou on observe Ie contraste entre ton H et ton non H, i.e. B, on est en droit d'en conclure que Ie wemcgbe comporte deux tons phonologique IHI et IBI et que BH est la realisation du ton IHI devant consonne voisee. tn.translation: Wemɛgbe presents the following tones: L, H, M, HL and LH. … Insofar as one observes the contrast between H tone and non-H tone, i.e. L, one is entitled to conclude that Wemɛgbe has two phonological tones /H/ and /L/ and that LH is the realisation of /H/ before a voiced consonant. … One is thus entitled to say that Wemɛgbe opposes an H tone to a non-H tone, symbolised respectively by H and B (L). The other tones, namely HL, M and LH, will be considered allotones of these two basic tones, and the task is to bring out the tonal rules of their realisation.

The placement of stress in Ojibwa (including Saulteaux) can be satisfactorily explained in a fairly straightforward fashion and there can be several stressed syllables within a word. There are three basic rules for stress assignment (as put forward by Voorhis et al 1976 and Cote 1984): 1) Each syllable with a long vowel will be stressed. 2) The last syllable of every word is obligatorily stressed. 3) Every second syllable in a sequence of syllables with short vowels will be stressed

5022.prule: Conflict between the two reachable first-hand descriptions. Miller 2018 (eight Manitoba Saulteaux speakers, 24 h of recordings, impressionistic): the only consistent prominence is on the final syllable of every noun and verb (rise in pitch and intensity), in isolation and inside sentences; no consistent primary or secondary stress elsewhere, and neither the traditional exhaustive-foot analysis nor Hayes' non-exhaustive analysis predicts what is heard; the author leaves open whether final prominence is word stress or a boundary effect. 5023.prule: Stratum-conditioned, hence lexically determined, word stress. Hebrew/Aramaic-component words (the whole of Weinberg's material) are 'gewöhnlich' stressed on the penultimate syllable, the Ashkenazic retraction from the Hebrew final syllable (berochaus < berakhót); the lexicon marks stress on a headword only when another syllable of a Hebrew word carries it (e.g. aumerbart), and the stress of a word in isolation is 'normalerweise fest' or varies with register (informal penult vs formal 'grammatische Betonung', berochaus ~ berochaus). The Germanic component is outside Weinberg's material; Katz 1993's pan-Yiddish statement gives it root-bound stress. No syllable-count or weight rule covers the language: position follows the word's component, the register, and, within the Hebrew component, the individual word.

5025.heavy: Carried text (LAPSyD on Watters 2002: 23-24): 'final long syllables' as against 'monomoraic syllables'; the primary's wording of 'long' is not in the carried text. Watters' own weight definition, first-hand in the 2003 sketch (Watters 2003: 686, excerpt): "The basic syllable in Kham is (C)(G)V(X), where ‘G’ is a glide and ‘*X’ is a consonant or a vowel. Only the nucleus is obligatory. The presence of a glide adds no weight to the syllable. Weight is determined solely by the rhyme; the presence of X always creates a heavy syllable. Where X is a vowel of the same quality as V, the result is a long vowel (V:), and where X is a vowel of different quality, the result is a diphthong (VV). Where X is a consonant, V is necessarily short. In terms of syllable weight and rhythm groups, then, V:, VV, and VC have the same weight — all are bimoraic. The minimal word in Kham is bimoraic, while the minimal syllable is monomoraic." So a non-monomoraic ('long') syllable in Watters' terms is any bimoraic rhyme: V:, VV or VC; hence CVV+CVC rather than CVV alone. Watters 1971: 57 (about pitch, not stress) groups CVC and CV: the same way: "Any CVC or CV: syllable in a poly-syllabic stem is higher in pitch than an otherwise identical CV syllable."
5025.dflt: no discernible stress in bisyllabic/polysyllabic words of monomoraic syllables, except that trisyllabic forms show discernible stress on the final syllable
5025.prule: Non-contrastive stress conditioned by syllable length (Watters 2002: 23-24): stress falls on the long syllable, whether it is the final syllable (phətú: 'wool coat') or, where the first syllable is long ('which is somewhat rare'), on that long syllable rather than the final one (ká:sa 'lightly', phó:sa 'lung', bé:pari 'trader'); in trisyllabic morphemes of open short syllables stress is on the final syllable (buchulá 'adze', bokolá 'tree bark'); in bisyllabic morphemes of open short syllables there is no discernible stress placement (kata, baza, gohga). Stress 'is not to be equated with high pitch'; tone (melody x register) is the contrastive word prosody. LAPSyD's summary adds that Kham 'is interpreted as having no function for stress' and that 'these perceptions of stress may be illusory' (wording not found in the book's indexed text).

The domain of tone is the phonological word... In general, the first morpheme of a word determines the voice register of the word, and the last morpheme of a word determines the pitch pattern of the word." 5030.prule: No word-stress rule is stated by any first-hand source. Hedding 2022 says the stress pattern of SMPM remains to be determined: final stress is 'plausible' (rising tones are confined to word-final position) but he offers a historical explanation for that restriction 'without appealing to word stress'; at the phrase level neither noun nor adjective is more prominent (phonological phrases possibly unheaded). Eischens & Bennett 2025 posit a bimoraic foot right-aligned to the prosodic word but leave open 'whether feet are taken to be trochaic or iambic', i.e. whether the stressed mora is penultimate or final. tn.quote: There are at least five phonemic tones in SMPM, with three level tones and at least two contour tones. The three level tones are High tone (marked with an acute accent á), Mid tone (no diacritic), and Low tone (marked with a grave accent à). There is one phonemic rising tone, which rises from Low to High (marked with a hacek ǎ), and at least one falling tone (marked with a circumflex accent â). ... The mora is the tone-bearing unit, and any one of SMPM’s five tones may appear on a mono-moraic vowel (Peters, 2018).
tn.cite: Eischens, Ben & Andrew A. Hedding. 2024. San Martín Peras Mixtec (Illustration of the IPA). JIPA 54(2): 811–852, §3.1, §3.3–3.4; with Hedding 2022 PhD diss. UCSC §3.1.2 (p. 99) and pp. 176–177 fn. 13
tn.note: Five tones (H, M, L, rising, falling) carried by the mora and cross-classified with phonation type; how many falling tones contrast (HL, ML, HM) is left open; word stress undetermined (Hedding 2022).

5031.dq: There are three stress and or pitch patterns in the dialect of Mecha. Pattern One: A word ending in a short vowel has a primary stress and a high pitch on the penultimate ... Pattern Two: Any word ending in a consonant or in a long vowel has a primary stress and a high pitch on the ultimate syllable ... Pattern Three: In any monosyllabic word, the syllable has a primary stress and a high pitch.

5031.heavy: a word 'ending in a consonant or in a long vowel' (closed final syllable or final long vowel) takes final stress; a word 'ending in a short vowel' takes penultimate stress. Weight is consulted on the final syllable only; a non-final long vowel does not attract primary stress in Wako's data (dè:mán, barbá:de). Dejene 2010 (Wello) differs for consonant-final words, where a non-final long-vowel syllable takes the primary (áatàm).
5031.dflt: penultimate (any word ending in a short vowel)
5031.prule: Primary stress (realised with high pitch) on the final syllable when the word ends in a consonant or a long vowel; on the penultimate when the word ends in a short vowel; monosyllables stressed. Only the final syllable's weight is consulted (dè:mán 'they went' has a long-vowel penult but final stress; barbá:de 'I or he wanted' is penult-stressed because the word ends in a short vowel).
5031.srule: Three degrees of stress (primary, secondary, weak); secondary stress always carries low pitch and falls on syllables preceding the primary: in words ending in a consonant or long vowel (primary on the ultimate) 'on any preceding syllable' - the examples mark every pre-tonic syllable (bìšá:n 'water', ʔìnǰìrá:n 'lice', dè:mán 'they went'); in words ending in a short vowel (primary on the penult) 'on a preceding syllable if there is any' (examples barbá:de, galgála carry no secondary mark). No secondary after the primary in citation forms; no alternating rhythm described.
5031.quote: There are three degrees of stress - primary, secondary and weak stress, and there are two levels of pitch - high and low in Mecha dialect. It is difficult to treat stress and pitch separately, because the primary stress and high pitch occur inseparably on the same syllable and the secondary stress and the low pitch occur simultaneously on the same syllable in their respective patterns. Stress and pitch are phonetic in the sense that they are predictable from their phonological environments. They also have a grammatical status in the sense that they signal grammatical meanings. 5032.dq: 10.1 Introduction. In this chapter, I describe word stress in Maaloula Aramaic. I will begin by reviewing and revising the word-stress algorithm which has been known since Bergsträsser (1915).
5032.dloc: Ch. 10 'Stress', §10.1 p. 214 and §10.2 'Stress algorithm' pp. 214-216; algorithm (1) p. 214, exception discussion and examples (2)-(3) p. 215, revised moraic algorithm (4) and window statement p. 216
5032.heavy: Final syllable heavy = 'has a long vowel or ends with two consonants or a geminate' (bimoraic; a single final consonant is extrametrical: ray.ˈšay.⟨n⟩, so final CVC is light). Penultimate syllable heavy = bimoraic: long vowel (ḥaẓ.ˈẓū.ra) or closed CVC (ˈṯar.ʕa, ṯi.na.ˈġel.ča). Light = 'the final syllable is CV or CVC, and the penultimate syllable is CV' (p. 215).
5032.dflt: Penultimate in disyllabic words; antepenultimate in words of three or more syllables (rule 4c, p. 216: 'Otherwise stress the penultimate syllable in disyllabic words and stress the antepenultimate syllable in polysyllabic words').
5032.prule: Weight-sensitive stress in a three-syllable window at the right word edge: stress the final syllable if it is bimoraic (long vowel, or closed by two consonants or a geminate; a single final consonant is extrametrical); otherwise stress the penultimate if it is bimoraic (long vowel or closed CVC); otherwise stress the penult in disyllables and the antepenult in words of three or more syllables (regardless of the antepenult's weight). Bergsträsser 1915: XXI and Jastrow 1997: 336 state the same final-if-heavy-else-penult rule; Eid's corpus study adds the light-light antepenult clause.
5032.srule: Not mentioned in Eid 2024 (ch. 10 'Stress', pp. 214-236, read in full; a full-text search of the book finds no secondary or rhythmic stress; p. 15 'has one main stress' is a wordhood criterion only). Earlier first-hand mention, no placement: Bergsträsser 1915 records a 'Gegenton' (counter-stress, marked with the same acute as the main stress) which verb forms with the double object suffix -lle 'almost always' carry, and after which allegro gemination can occur as after a main-stressed syllable; he gives no rule for where it falls.

5033.prule: Stress falls on the last syllable of the word by default; words with non-final stress are marked individually with an acute in the list. Ten marked entries in all (Eastern column unless noted): búa / Western (búa) 'jaguar', búa he / (búa he) 'puma', hoyóro 'kidney', krátsa 'cockroach' (p. 167); mánte (beside unmarked variant mande; Western (mande)) 'john crow', marára 'bad, ugly, stingy', máta (Western (mata)) 'two' (p. 168); tapúa 'strings used by the diviner', tsenam máta 'forty', tséle (Western (tsere)) 'chile pepper' (p. 169). Among the parenthesised Western forms only (búa) and (búa he) carry a mark; every other polysyllabic Western form on pp. 167-170 is unmarked, i.e. final-stressed under the convention -- e.g. (arba), (askip), (pubö), (abrugay), (kamuey), (mon duvera), (hobi), (hiktsa), (huktsa), (hubue), (kansong), (kastre), (latsak), (dara), (lubu), (luru), (koko), (korok), (harek), (hene), (keke), (uruk), (mande), (mata), (tsere), (yurubana) -- including (mande), (mata), (tsere), whose Eastern counterparts mánte, máta, tséle are marked non-final. In two-word entries the mark sits on one word (búa he, tsenam máta), i.e. the convention is applied per word. Stated as the transcription convention governing a c. 1921 elicited vocabulary, not as an analysed phonological rule.

5040.dq: Wolaitta has a restricted high tone-accent marking in the citation form of various categories. All lexical nouns and adjectives have only one high tone-accent. (p. 114; phrase-level accent is treated separately in sect. 4: 'high tone-accent is always marked on the modifier(s), but not on the head category in the phrase', p. 114)
5040.dloc: pp. 113-114 (sect. 1, arguments against the stress analyses and conclusion), 115-116 (sect. 2.1 simple nouns, ex. 3-6), 118-119 (sect. 2.3 summary: mora marking, positional contrasts), 122-123 (sect. 3.2.1 accented vs unaccented verb roots)., pp. 3-4, 5-6, 8-9, 12-13
5040.heavy: not applicable: 'Vowel quantity and quality do not affect tone-accent assignment. All five vowels of the language can carry tone-accent' (p. 118); long vowels may or may not be accented (ex. 11)
5040.prule: Mora-counting tone-accent (pitch-accent) system, explicitly not stress: each simple word carries one culminative high tone-accent realized as an invariant H (on an accented long vowel the second mora bears it, giving a rise). In nouns and adjectives the H falls lexically on the final or the penultimate mora, not predictable from word class or meaning; verb roots are lexically accented (H on the root's first vowel) or unaccented (H on the inflectional suffix; final mora of infinitival -etta).
5040.srule: None: the source denies word stress altogether and any primary/secondary gradation ('there is no such gradable distinction in prominence between two or more accented syllables in a word'); a simple word has one high tone-accent, and morphologically complex words (derived nominals, jussive/negative verbs) may carry two or more equal high tone-accents, which are tone-accents, not secondary stresses.
5040.quote: In previous studies Wolaitta has been described as a stress language (cf. Adams [1983] and Yitbarek [1983]). ... First, in accented long vowels the second mora receives tone-accent. This would not be possible in a stress language since the domain of stress is the syllable as a whole. ... Second, derived complex words have more than one high tone-accent. ... there is no such gradable distinction in prominence between two or more accented syllables in a word. [p. 113] Thus, Wolaitta does not belong to the category of stress languages. ... All lexical nouns and adjectives have only one high tone…
5040.loc: pp. 113-114 (sect. 1, arguments against the stress analyses and conclusion), 115-116 (sect. 2.1 simple nouns, ex. 3-6), 118-119 (sect. 2.3 summary: mora marking, positional contrasts), 122-123 (sect. 3.2.1 accented vs unaccented verb roots)., pp. 3-4, 5-6, 8-9, 12-13
5040.idn: Wolaitta (no dialect named; author's own first-language speech); data: south-central Ethiopia; data = the author's (Azeb Amha, Leiden University) own speech as a first-language speaker; no locality or collection dates stated (published 1996)
5040.exq_: A few trisyllabic and quadrisyllabic words constitute exceptions to the final or penultimate mora tone-accent marking, having the high tone-accent on the ante-penultimate mora, as illustrated in (5). ... There are only a few words of this type in Wolaitta, each ending with /-nta/, /-tta/ or /-puna/…
5040.tone: The source rejects the stress analyses of Adams 1983 and Yitbarek 1983 ('Wolaitta does not belong to the category of stress languages', p. 114) on two grounds: the H sits on the second mora of an accented long vowel (a rise; mora, not syllable, is the domain, cf. Hyman 1981 on Somali as a tonal-accent language with an invariant H), and derived complex words carry more than one H with no gradable prominence (p. 113). One H per simple word in citation form; penultimate position takes only H, final position H or (object pronouns only) falling (p. 119). Independent concurrence: Wakasa 2014, Nilo-Ethiopian Studies 19, p. 32: 'Pitch can be used distinctively. There are minimal pairs distinguished only by pitch, such as dooríis ‘he chose’ and dóóriis ‘he piled up’... Where the high pitch is allocated in the word is determined for each conjugated (inflected) form of each word, and the place is not completely predictable', and within an intonation group only the first word realizes its high pitch.

5041.tone: The source equivocates: the feature is introduced as 'vowel tone--or vowel stress--/´/' and treated as a vowel phoneme alongside length /: and nasalization /ⁿ/ (Table II, p. 82; text p. 83). No pitch shapes, no number of tones, no stress rule are given; the only other use of the word is the allophonic environment 'utterance-initial stressed syllable' for implosive [d] (p. 83). The Appendix A marking is privative (5 of c. 70 Wodani items marked, always the final vowel), which fits a lexical high tone / pitch accent better than culminative word stress. Voorhoeve 1975: 408 (Central and Western TNG Phylum Languages, PL C-38; saved), summarising this same paper, states 'Vowel nasalization is distinctive; the language is tonal.' Reading lexical (lexically contrastive stress) is the defensible alternative if the 'stress' branch of the source's own hedge is taken; the two readings differ only in label, not in content (no placement rule either way).
